tagline: From canyon country to a tribal college and the Navajo capital.
intro: Navajo Route 64 connects Chinle and Tsaile, just outside Canyon de Chelly National Monument. The monument’s canyons were cut by streams rising in the Chuska Mountains to the east.

In 1968, the Navajo Nation chartered Navajo Community College, now Diné College. A survey recommended the Tsaile–Wheatfields area for its water, forests and lakes. Classes at the permanent Tsaile campus began in October 1973.

Chinle is the gateway community for Canyon de Chelly; Tsaile holds Diné College’s main campus. Farther south, Route 12 links Navajo, New Mexico, with Fort Defiance, Arizona. Window Rock is served by Indian Route 12 and takes its name from a sandstone window formation.

moments.title: Chinle
moments.text: Chinle’s Navajo name means “flowing out,” describing the water leaving Canyon de Chelly. A trading post began here in a tent in 1882, and a full-sized camp had developed by 1885. The town serves as the gateway to Canyon de Chelly National Monument, established in 1931 to preserve archaeological sites and the record of human history. The canyon also remains a place of residence: the monument lies entirely on Navajo tribal land and contains a residential community. Local government is based at the Chinle Chapter House, which serves as a town hall with elected officers.

moments.title: Tsaile
moments.text: Most buildings at Diné College’s Tsaile campus were built with eight sides, echoing the traditional Navajo hogan. The college opened in 1968 as Navajo Community College, the first college established by Native Americans for Native Americans. Its first home was temporary, at Rough Rock Community School. The Board of Regents chose the Tsaile–Wheatfields area after a survey recommended its plentiful water, forests and lakes. Students began classes here in October 1973; the campus was dedicated the following May. In 1997, the institution adopted the name Diné College to better represent its role in education for Diné/Navajo people.
moments.notice: The campus buildings’ octagonal shapes echo the traditional eight-sided Navajo hogan.

moments.title: Window Rock
moments.text: The sandstone window that names Window Rock stands north of the Navajo government administration buildings. The city serves as the capital of the Navajo Nation. John Collier, Commissioner of Indian Affairs, chose the site for the Navajo Central Agency, the Bureau of Indian Affairs’ connection to the nation. His proposal to use its ceremonial name met resistance; the BIA instead chose the name of the rock formation. The government complex houses the Navajo Nation Council and Supreme Court, along with the President’s and Vice President’s offices. The Navajo Nation Museum is also here, with a permanent home built in 1997 in a modern Navajo hogan style.
moments.notice: The sandstone window formation is north of the Navajo government administration buildings.
